title: Overview of Research Progress and Applications of Experimental Models of Colorectal Cancer

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A useful point of departure for colorectal cancer (CRC) model systems is the recognition that no single platform captures the full malignant phenotype. CRC progression reflects the acquisition of core cancer capabilities together with dynamic interactions among tumor cells, stromal elements, vasculature, and immune compartments; these interacting layers are especially critical for invasion, dissemination, and therapy resistance ref [1], ref [2], ref [23]. Accordingly, experimental models should be viewed not simply as substitutes for human disease, but as complementary systems that selectively preserve particular biological dimensions of CRC.

This perspective is particularly important for modeling metastasis, the major cause of CRC mortality. Conceptual frameworks such as the 'seed and soil' hypothesis and more recent metastasis models emphasize that successful colonization depends both on intrinsic properties of disseminated tumor cells and on permissive microenvironments in distant organs ref [6], ref [8], ref [14]. For CRC, this means that reductionist systems are well suited to dissect tumor-cell-autonomous programs, whereas orthotopic, metastatic, or immune-competent platforms are required to study organotropism, metastatic bottlenecks, and ecological constraints imposed by the host tissue context ref [2], ref [23].

In parallel, immune regulation has become indispensable in CRC modeling. Clinical and experimental evidence indicates that T-cell states influence early metastatic control and patient outcome, while pathways such as TGFβ can actively promote immune evasion during colon cancer metastasis ref [19], ref [31]. These observations justify the growing emphasis on model systems that retain functional tumor-immune crosstalk, and they provide the conceptual basis for the comparative discussion of in vitro, organoid, xenograft, and genetically engineered CRC models in the following subsections.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Metastasis-focused CRC models are particularly valuable because they capture biological processes that are poorly represented in conventional primary-tumor systems, including stemness plasticity, stromal dependence, immune remodeling, and organ-specific colonization. Functional studies have shown that metastatic initiation can depend on tumor-cell subpopulations marked by CD44v6 and on context-dependent behavior of Lgr5+ stem-like cells, indicating that lineage state and cellular plasticity must be considered when selecting xenograft, orthotopic, or lineage-tracing platforms for CRC research ref [23], ref [26].

These models also highlight the necessity of incorporating the tumor microenvironment. Stromal TGF-β programs were shown to be required for metastasis initiation, while bidirectional signaling between CRC cells and tumor-associated macrophages supports mesenchymal circulating tumor cells and dissemination ref [12], ref [25]. Likewise, cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosomes can enhance stemness, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, metastasis, and chemotherapy resistance, underscoring the utility of co-culture systems, stromal-humanized xenografts, and metastasis assays that preserve non-malignant compartments ref [28].

At the same time, newer model-integrated analytical approaches are refining mechanistic resolution. Single-cell profiling of CRC liver metastasis has revealed a dynamic spatiotemporal immune landscape, supporting the use of models that permit immune-context interrogation rather than tumor-cell-only readouts ref [27]. Molecular perturbation studies further demonstrate that noncoding regulators, such as circular RNA CCDC66, can promote colon cancer growth and metastasis, emphasizing the value of genetically engineered and RNA-focused systems for dissecting metastatic drivers beyond protein-coding genes ref [36]. Together, these metastasis-relevant platforms provide complementary views of CRC progression and therapeutic vulnerability.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Metastasis-oriented CRC models are designed to capture dynamic processes that conventional proliferation assays often miss, including epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), invasion, dissemination, and colonization of distant organs. In this context, model selection should be guided by the biological question: reductionist systems are useful for dissecting motility programs and EMT regulation, whereas multicellular platforms are required to study stromal crosstalk and metastatic niche formation. Reviews on CRC EMT and broader metastasis systems biology emphasize that no single model reproduces the full metastatic cascade, making complementary use of 2D migration assays, 3D invasion systems, organotypic cultures, and in vivo dissemination models essential ref [17], ref [37].

Simple experimental organisms and engineered migration platforms have been particularly informative for conserved mechanisms of cell motility, polarity, and collective invasion, offering tractable settings for hypothesis generation before validation in mammalian CRC systems ref [25]. At higher biological complexity, the tumor microenvironment becomes indispensable: stromal cells, extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory mediators, and organ-specific cues critically regulate invasion and metastatic outgrowth, so co-culture and tissue-mimetic models are needed to represent these interactions ref [36]. Single-cell approaches further show that metastatic competence is distributed across heterogeneous tumor and stromal cell states rather than a uniform cancer-cell phenotype, supporting experimental designs that preserve intratumoral diversity ref [18].

Immune-informed metastatic models are increasingly important in CRC because neutrophils and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) can promote tumor cell survival, extravasation, and colonization, phenomena that are invisible in tumor-cell-only systems ref [16], ref [23]. Such findings argue for syngeneic, humanized, or ex vivo platforms that incorporate innate immune components when evaluating anti-metastatic therapies. Overall, metastasis research in CRC benefits most from an integrated modeling strategy that links mechanistic simplicity with multicellular and systems-level complexity ref [36], ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A particularly important class of CRC experimental systems is composed of metastasis-oriented models that preserve tumor–microenvironment interactions, especially for studying liver colonization. These platforms are valuable because they capture immune remodeling, stromal support, and organ-specific adaptation that are largely inaccessible in simplified in vitro assays. Comparative analyses of primary colorectal tumors and matched liver metastases have shown linked but remodeled immune phenotypes across sites, supporting the use of paired primary–metastatic model systems to interrogate metastatic niche evolution rather than tumor-cell-intrinsic behavior alone [4].

Within such models, several studies highlight macrophage-centered mechanisms as tractable experimental readouts. Gut microbiota-driven signaling can promote metastasis through cathepsin K secretion and TLR4-dependent M2 macrophage polarization, indicating that models retaining microbial or innate immune inputs are especially informative for CRC progression studies [17]. Similarly, exosome-based communication has been shown to enhance liver metastasis via CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling and macrophage M2 polarization, while the lncRNA RPPH1 promotes metastatic behavior through exosome-mediated macrophage education [24, 28]. These findings underscore the utility of co-culture systems, orthotopic implantation, and liver metastasis assays that permit dynamic analysis of extracellular vesicles and immune-cell polarization.

Stromal and inflammatory components further broaden the relevance of these metastasis models. Mesenchymal stem cells can enhance colon cancer growth and dissemination, illustrating how stromal-cell incorporation increases the biological fidelity of experimental platforms [16]. In parallel, direct activation of tumor-cell TLR4 signaling by LPS increases beta1-integrin-dependent adhesion and liver metastatic potential, emphasizing that models incorporating inflammatory cues can reveal mechanisms of vascular arrest and organ seeding [38]. Collectively, these systems are most useful when the research question concerns metastatic competence, immune education, and liver tropism, although their greater complexity can reduce standardization and throughput compared with reductionist cell-autonomous models [4, 16, 17, 24, 28, 38].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Model Systems for Colorectal Cancer Research - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Metastasis-oriented CRC models constitute a distinct experimental tier because they are designed to interrogate dissemination, colonization, and organ-specific outgrowth rather than only primary tumor formation. In practice, these systems commonly combine highly invasive human CRC cell lines, orthotopic implantation, splenic or portal-vein injection, and liver-colonization assays to quantify metastatic competence and to functionally test candidate drivers. Such models have been instrumental in showing that metastasis is not merely a late by-product of tumor growth, but a selectable phenotype governed by adhesion, motility, EMT-like plasticity, and niche adaptation ref [19], ref [21], ref [26].

Representative studies illustrate how these platforms uncover mechanistic mediators of metastatic behavior. CXCL5 was shown to enhance CRC metastasis through ERK/Elk-1/Snail and AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin signaling, highlighting the utility of in vivo metastatic assays for linking secreted factors to invasion and colonization ref [19]. Similarly, enforced expression of L1-CAM and ADAM10 increased metastatic capacity in colon cancer models, while later work further identified L1CAM-positive regenerative cell states as a source of metastasis-initiating cells, underscoring how lineage plasticity can be captured in transplantation-based systems ref [21], ref [26]. Hypoxia-adapted metabolic dependencies are also resolvable in these models, as glutaminase 1 was found to be required for tumor growth, invasion, and metastatic colonization ref [38].

A major advance has been the incorporation of stromal and extracellular-vesicle components into metastatic model design. Cancer-derived exosomal HSPC111 was reported to promote liver metastasis by reprogramming lipid metabolism in cancer-associated fibroblasts, demonstrating that contemporary CRC metastasis models can dissect bidirectional tumor–stroma communication at the premetastatic and colonization stages ref [23]. Collectively, these systems are particularly valuable for evaluating metastatic initiators, organotropism, and therapeutic vulnerabilities, although their reductionist nature means that no single platform fully captures the evolutionary and immunological complexity of spontaneous human CRC metastasis ref [19], ref [23], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been central to defining colorectal cancer (CRC) evolution as a stepwise acquisition of malignant capabilities, in which sustained proliferation, invasion, metastatic dissemination, and immune escape emerge through interacting genetic and non-genetic programs rather than a purely linear mutational sequence ref [1]. In this framework, model systems that permit controlled perturbation of epithelial cells have been especially useful for linking molecular state transitions to specific stages of CRC progression.

A major theme revealed by these models is the plasticity of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT). Rather than a binary switch, EMT often proceeds through intermediate states that combine migratory, survival, and colonization traits, thereby supporting dissemination while preserving adaptability ref [17]. This plasticity is closely connected to stem-like behavior and therapeutic resistance, forming an EMT–cancer stem cell axis that helps explain relapse and progression in advanced disease ref [15]. Mechanistically, regulatory circuits such as reciprocal repression between ZEB1 and the miR-200 family stabilize alternative epithelial and mesenchymal states and provide a tractable module for modeling phenotypic switching in CRC-like contexts ref [24].

Noncoding RNAs add another layer to CRC pathogenesis models. The metastasis-associated lncRNA HOTAIR demonstrated that lncRNAs can actively reprogram chromatin states to favor malignant progression ref [36], while miRNAs illustrate how small RNAs couple differentiation and invasion programs. let-7 limits self-renewal and tumorigenicity in cancer cells ref [21], whereas miR-21 directly promotes invasive and metastatic behavior in CRC through post-transcriptional repression of tumor suppressive targets such as PDCD4 ref [22]. Finally, genetically reconstituted colon cancer metastasis models have shown that TGFβ signaling can drive immune evasion during metastatic progression ref [31], highlighting how cell-state plasticity and microenvironmental adaptation co-evolve during CRC advancement.

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been particularly informative in linking colorectal cancer (CRC) progression to epithelial–mesenchymal plasticity rather than to a fixed EMT endpoint. Conceptual and functional studies indicate that reversible transitions between epithelial and mesenchymal states enable dissemination, survival under stress, and metastatic outgrowth, making plasticity a dynamic driver of tumor evolution rather than a simple binary switch ref [11]. In CRC models, this plasticity is closely coupled to the acquisition of stem-like traits, thereby connecting local invasion with regenerative capacity at distant sites ref [23], ref [26].

Lineage-tracing and transplantation systems further show that stem-cell states are context dependent during CRC progression. Lgr5+ cells are important for primary tumor maintenance, yet metastatic lesions can be initiated or sustained through state transitions that regenerate stemness after dissemination, emphasizing that metastatic competence is not restricted to a static cellular subset ref [26]. Consistently, CD44v6 marks both constitutive and reprogrammed cancer stem cells that drive colon cancer metastasis, illustrating how experimental reprogramming models can capture the emergence of metastasis-initiating phenotypes during disease evolution ref [23].

Microenvironmental models add another layer by showing that phenotypic plasticity is actively instructed by stromal signaling. Crosstalk with tumor-associated macrophages promotes mesenchymal circulating tumor cell formation and metastatic seeding in CRC, while cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosomes enhance stemness, EMT features, metastasis, and chemoresistance ref [25], ref [28]. Noncoding RNA models extend this framework: circular RNA CCDC66 exerts noncoding functions that support colon cancer growth and metastasis, indicating that RNA-mediated regulation can stabilize aggressive cell states during progression ref [36]. Together, these studies position CRC evolution as a highly plastic process shaped by reciprocal interactions among stemness programs, stromal cues, and noncoding regulators ref [11], ref [25], ref [28], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Experimental models have been especially informative for linking colorectal cancer (CRC) evolution to phenotypic plasticity, particularly the interconversion between epithelial, mesenchymal, and stem-like states. In CRC, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) is now understood less as a binary switch than as a dynamic program that enhances invasion, dissemination, and therapy tolerance while preserving the capacity for later metastatic outgrowth ref [17]. Single-cell analyses further show that metastatic competence emerges from heterogeneous cellular subpopulations rather than uniform clonal behavior, underscoring the importance of models that resolve state transitions at high resolution ref [18].

A major advance from organoid, xenograft, and lineage-tracing systems is the demonstration that EMT programs intersect with cancer stem cell (CSC) traits and stress-adaptation pathways. Conceptual frameworks of metastasis stem cells suggest that only a subset of tumor cells can couple migratory capacity with long-term tumor-propagating potential ref [26]. Consistently, work on EMT, CSCs, and autophagy supports a coordinated axis in which plasticity-promoting programs facilitate survival during detachment, transit, and colonization ref [29]. Marker-based studies, including CD44/CD24 and ALDH1, have therefore been used in experimental CRC-related settings to operationalize stem-like subpopulations and to compare their contributions to tumor initiation, metastatic seeding, and relapse ref [33].

Noncoding RNA-centered models add a further regulatory layer to this evolutionary process. Long noncoding RNAs can modulate chromatin state, EMT regulators, and metastatic signaling networks, thereby stabilizing aggressive phenotypes or enabling reversible transitions under microenvironmental pressure ref [43]. At a systems level, these observations support viewing CRC progression as an emergent property of interacting molecular circuits rather than isolated pathways ref [37]. Together, experimental models indicate that CRC pathogenesis involves continuous selection among heterogeneous cell states, with EMT, stemness, autophagy, and noncoding RNA regulation acting as coupled determinants of metastatic evolution ref [18], ref [17], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis have increasingly clarified how immune remodeling and intercellular communication drive molecular evolution during dissemination, particularly to the liver. Comparative profiling of primary CRC and matched liver metastases indicates that metastatic progression is accompanied by a linked but reshaped immune phenotype, supporting the view that tumor evolution is not purely cancer cell-intrinsic but co-determined by adaptive changes in the metastatic niche ref [27]. These observations have been reinforced by model systems showing that inflammatory signals can directly enhance metastatic competence of CRC cells.

Mechanistically, TLR4-centered signaling emerges as a recurrent axis connecting microbial products, tumor cells, and myeloid polarization. In CRC cells, LPS-induced TLR4 activation increases beta1-integrin-dependent adhesion and promotes liver metastasis, indicating that innate inflammatory sensing can directly alter adhesive and colonization behavior ref [38]. At the microenvironmental level, gut microbiota-stimulated cathepsin K secretion has been shown to drive TLR4-dependent M2 macrophage polarization, thereby facilitating metastatic progression ref [17]. Together, these models support a stepwise scheme in which inflammation not only selects for more aggressive phenotypes but also constructs a permissive metastatic ecosystem.

Noncoding RNA-mediated intercellular transfer further refines this process. Exosome-based models demonstrate that CRC-derived miRNAs downstream of the CXCL12/CXCR4 axis promote liver metastasis by enhancing macrophage M2 polarization ref [24]. Similarly, the lncRNA RPPH1 promotes metastasis both through interaction with TUBB3 in tumor cells and through exosome-mediated induction of M2 macrophages ref [28]. Collectively, these studies position exosomal cargos as evolutionary effectors that couple intrinsic transcriptional or cytoskeletal programs to extrinsic immune reprogramming, thereby stabilizing metastatic traits across disease stages ref [27], ref [17], ref [24], ref [28], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Modeling the Molecular Pathogenesis and Evolution of Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major theme emerging from colorectal cancer (CRC) models is that metastatic competence is not a fixed property of bulk tumor cells, but is concentrated in metastasis-initiating and stem-like subpopulations that retain marked phenotypic plasticity. Conceptual and experimental work has linked cancer stem cells to dissemination, dormancy, and colonization, while emphasizing that these capacities are shaped by the surrounding metastatic ecosystem rather than by cell-intrinsic programs alone ref [45], ref [29]. In CRC specifically, L1CAM-positive regenerative cells have been identified as a source of metastasis-initiating cells, extending earlier observations that enforced L1-CAM and ADAM10 expression can directly promote metastatic behavior in colon cancer models ref [26], ref [21].

These models further show that epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity and stemness are coordinated by signaling circuits that couple local invasion to outgrowth at distant sites. TGF-β has a central role in this transition by sustaining stem-like states, invasive behavior, and metastatic colonization in context-dependent fashion ref [18]. Complementing this, tumor-derived CXCL5 activates ERK/Elk-1/Snail and AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin pathways, providing a mechanistic link between inflammatory signaling, EMT-associated transcriptional reprogramming, and CRC metastasis ref [19]. Together, these findings support an evolutionary view in which metastatic clones emerge through reversible state transitions rather than simple linear selection.

Metastatic evolution in CRC also depends on metabolic adaptation and reciprocal stromal reprogramming. Hypoxia-induced glutaminase 1 expression enhances tumor growth, invasion, and metastatic colonization, indicating that nutrient utilization programs are integral to the acquisition of aggressive phenotypes ref [38]. In parallel, cancer-derived exosomal HSPC111 can remodel cancer-associated fibroblasts by rewiring lipid metabolism, thereby creating a permissive niche for liver metastasis ref [23]. Collectively, these models place stemness, signaling plasticity, metabolism, and microenvironmental education within a unified framework for understanding CRC progression from local tumor heterogeneity to successful metastatic seeding and expansion ref [45], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Experimental modeling of the colorectal cancer (CRC) microenvironment has increasingly moved beyond tumor cell–intrinsic views of metastasis toward integrated “seed and soil” frameworks, in which stromal composition, matrix architecture, and host organ context jointly determine metastatic competence ref [51], ref [3]. In this setting, co-culture systems, matrix-tunable 3D assays, and orthotopic in vivo models have been especially valuable for dissecting how CRC cells engage fibroblasts, endothelial barriers, and immune compartments during local invasion and dissemination ref [3], ref [9].

Among stromal elements, fibroblast-centered models have shown that activated fibroblasts are not passive bystanders but major organizers of metastatic niches through secretion of growth factors, cytokines, and matrix-remodeling enzymes ref [9]. Parallel studies of extracellular matrix remodeling further indicate that collagen organization, proteolytic remodeling, and stiffness-dependent signaling directly regulate invasion, survival under mechanical stress, and outgrowth at distant sites ref [26]. Integrin-focused experimental systems have complemented these findings by demonstrating that tumor cell adhesion receptors function at nearly every step of progression, from migration and intravasation to vascular arrest and colonization, thereby linking matrix state to metastatic behavior ref [38].

Recent CRC-relevant models have also highlighted extracellular vesicles as microenvironmental educators. Exosome-based studies support the concept that vesicular cargo can prime distant tissues, reshape stromal and immune responses, and contribute to organotropism before overt metastases emerge ref [28]. Notably, exosomal integrin signatures have been implicated in directing organ-specific metastatic seeding, providing an experimentally tractable mechanism for pre-metastatic niche specification ref [8]. In parallel, genetically reconstituted colon cancer metastasis models have shown that TGFβ signaling can enforce immune evasion within metastatic ecosystems, underscoring the need for models that simultaneously capture stromal, immune, and vesicle-mediated regulation of CRC spread ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Experimental modeling of colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis has increasingly focused on bidirectional signaling between tumor cells and stromal or immune compartments. In organoid co-culture and mouse transplantation systems, metastatic initiation was shown to depend not only on intrinsic epithelial programs but also on a stromal TGF-β response, highlighting fibroblast-state remodeling as a necessary component of dissemination competence rather than a passive consequence of tumor growth ref [9]. Complementing this view, studies of cancer stem-like populations demonstrated that CD44v6-positive cells and dynamically regulated Lgr5-positive cells make distinct contributions to metastatic seeding and outgrowth, providing experimental support for models in which stemness is plastic and microenvironmentally instructed during the metastatic cascade ref [10], ref [12].

Immune-interaction models have further clarified how circulating and disseminated CRC cells are stabilized by host cells. Macrophage–tumor cell co-culture and in vivo metastasis assays showed that crosstalk with tumor-associated macrophages is required for the generation and persistence of mesenchymal circulating tumor cells, directly linking immune education to hematogenous spread ref [11]. Neutrophil extracellular trap-based models added another layer, showing that NET-derived DNA can promote metastatic colonization through CCDC25-dependent sensing by cancer cells, thereby functionally connecting inflammatory niches with organotropic capture of disseminated cells ref [53]. Single-cell mapping of CRC liver metastases has also revealed marked spatiotemporal immune reorganization, offering a framework for integrating reductionist models with the evolving cellular ecosystems of established metastatic lesions ref [13].

Extracellular-vesicle models bridge these stromal and immune processes by explaining how metastatic competence is transmitted at distance. General studies of exosome biology established their roles in intercellular communication, immune modulation, and niche conditioning ref [54]. In CRC-specific systems, cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosomes were shown to enhance epithelial–mesenchymal transition, stemness, metastasis, and chemotherapy resistance, illustrating how vesicle-mediated signaling can couple local microenvironmental remodeling to systemic progression ref [14]. Together, these models support a multistep view of CRC metastasis in which stromal activation, stem-cell plasticity, inflammatory trapping, and vesicle-based communication cooperatively generate a permissive pre-metastatic and metastatic niche.

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Experimental modeling of the colorectal cancer metastatic cascade increasingly centers on reconstruction of the pre-metastatic niche, where stromal remodeling, soluble metabolites, and extracellular vesicles condition distant organs before tumor-cell arrival. Across transwell co-cultures, organotypic matrices, and murine metastasis models, the tumor microenvironment has emerged not as a passive scaffold but as an active regulator of invasion, survival, and colonization ref [14], ref [36]. Systems-level analyses further support the view that metastatic competence arises from coordinated interactions among heterogeneous tumor-cell states and host tissues rather than from a purely tumor-intrinsic program ref [56], ref [37].

Among niche-building mechanisms, extracellular matrix remodeling is especially amenable to experimental interrogation, because matrix composition and stiffness can be manipulated in 3D culture and decellularized scaffold systems to test effects on colorectal cancer adhesion, migration, and outgrowth ref [14]. Parallel work on extracellular vesicle biology has shown that tumor-derived exosomes can reprogram distant organ microenvironments; although demonstrated in gastric cancer, exosomal EGFR-mediated conditioning of the liver provides an instructive paradigm for modeling how gastrointestinal tumors educate hepatic stromal compartments before metastatic seeding ref [12]. Such cross-cancer evidence has informed CRC liver metastasis models focused on exosome uptake, fibroblast activation, and endothelial permeability.

Immune components are likewise being incorporated into metastatic models. Neutrophils and neutrophil extracellular traps can be studied in co-culture, circulation-mimetic devices, and in vivo colonization assays to evaluate how innate immunity promotes tumor-cell arrest, survival, and metastatic outgrowth ref [16], ref [23]. Macrophage polarization is also shaped by tumor-derived metabolites; succinate-driven signaling illustrates how metabolic communication can bias macrophages toward pro-metastatic functions, offering a tractable framework for CRC models that link cancer metabolism to immune niche formation ref [19]. Together, these platforms are refining mechanistic understanding of organ-specific metastasis and identifying microenvironmental vulnerabilities that may be therapeutically targetable ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Experimental models of colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis have increasingly focused on immune and inflammatory components of the liver-tropic metastatic niche. Comparative analyses of paired primary CRC and liver metastases revealed linked but remodeled immune phenotypes, supporting the use of matched patient samples, syngeneic implantation systems, and metastatic mouse models to study how immune selection accompanies metastatic colonization rather than merely reflecting primary tumor biology ref [27]. These observations have helped position immune-context reconstruction as a core requirement in modeling CRC dissemination to the liver.

Several mechanistic studies further show that macrophage polarization is a tractable and recurrent node in CRC metastatic modeling. In vitro co-culture and in vivo metastasis assays demonstrated that gut microbiota-driven cathepsin K secretion promotes TLR4-dependent M2 macrophage polarization and enhances metastatic progression, functionally linking microbial signals to protumor immunity ref [17]. Likewise, tumor-derived extracellular vesicle models showed that exosome-encapsulated miRNAs amplify CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling to facilitate liver metastasis by skewing macrophages toward an M2 state ref [24], while lncRNA RPPH1 was found to promote metastasis both through tumor-intrinsic effects and through exosome-mediated induction of M2 macrophage polarization ref [28]. Together, these systems highlight how organotropic spread can be reconstructed through tumor–immune communication modules.

Inflammation-dependent adhesion models also clarify how circulating CRC cells acquire liver-seeding competence. Experimental stimulation with lipopolysaccharide showed that TLR4 activation in CRC cells increases β1-integrin-mediated adhesion and promotes liver metastasis, providing a mechanistic bridge between inflammatory signaling, vascular arrest, and secondary organ colonization ref [38]. When integrated with immune-phenotype mapping and exosome-based macrophage education models, these findings support a multistep framework in which microbial and inflammatory cues, vesicle signaling, and myeloid reprogramming cooperatively establish the pre-metastatic and metastatic liver microenvironment ref [27], ref [17], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models of the Tumor Microenvironment and Metastatic Cascade in Colorectal Cancer - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Experimental reconstruction of the late metastatic cascade in colorectal cancer increasingly focuses on metastasis-initiating cells and the permissive ecosystems that support their survival, seeding, and outgrowth at distant sites. Conceptual frameworks emphasizing metastasis as an ecological process have been particularly useful for interpreting organoid transplantation, lineage-tracing, and xenograft studies, in which only rare cellular states display durable colonization potential ref [59]. In CRC, this has been sharpened by evidence that L1CAM marks a regenerative program associated with metastasis-initiating competence, thereby linking epithelial injury-response states to successful metastatic re-expansion in vivo ref [26].

These cell-intrinsic programs are strongly conditioned by stromal and physical microenvironments modeled in co-culture systems, engineered matrices, and orthotopic or liver-colonization assays. Biophysical properties such as matrix stiffness, interstitial stress, and flow alter motility and invasive behavior, highlighting why reductionist 2D models incompletely capture metastatic fitness ref [16]. Cancer-associated fibroblasts are central components of these models because they remodel extracellular matrix, supply trophic cues, and facilitate invasion and dissemination ref [35]. Consistent with this, CRC-derived exosomal HSPC111 has been shown to reprogram lipid metabolism in fibroblasts and promote liver metastasis, illustrating how extracellular vesicle-based communication can be incorporated into pre-metastatic niche models ref [23].

Blood-borne dissemination and metastatic arrest are also shaped by systemic host components that can be modeled in circulation-mimetic assays and in vivo metastasis platforms. Platelets protect tumor cells, enhance vascular adhesion, and support extravasation, making them important but sometimes underrepresented elements of CRC metastasis models ref [20]. Parallel studies further show that tumor-derived CXCL5 drives EMT-associated and β-catenin-linked signaling to promote metastatic behavior ref [19], whereas hypoxia-induced glutaminase 1 supports growth, invasion, and metastatic colonization, underscoring how metabolic adaptation must be integrated into advanced microenvironmental models ref [38]. Together, these systems move CRC research from static descriptions of the tumor microenvironment toward experimentally testable models of metastatic ecosystem assembly.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Experimental CRC models are increasingly used to connect metastatic biology with actionable therapeutic vulnerabilities. In this context, organoid, genetically engineered, and metastasis-reconstitution systems have been especially informative for identifying pathway dependencies that are not apparent in conventional proliferation assays. For example, reconstituted colon cancer metastasis models showed that TGFβ signaling promotes immune evasion, supporting its value not only as a mechanistic axis but also as a candidate stratification marker for immunomodulatory combinations in metastatic CRC ref [31].

These platforms are also useful for dissecting phenotypic plasticity and therapy resistance. Although EMT is not invariably required for metastatic dissemination, experimental evidence indicates that EMT programs can confer pronounced chemoresistance, emphasizing why model systems that preserve dynamic cell-state transitions are important for drug testing and response prediction ref [32]. Likewise, studies of cancer stem cell–niche interactions highlight how metastatic colonization depends on reciprocal signals from the microenvironment, suggesting that therapeutic development should target both tumor-intrinsic stemness programs and supportive niche components ref [35].

Several candidate liabilities emerging from experimental models are directly relevant to precision oncology. Metastasis-initiating cells display targetable metabolic traits, including dependence on the fatty acid receptor CD36, which has been proposed as an intervention point to suppress metastatic outgrowth ref [37]. Integrin-centered signaling, which regulates adhesion, invasion, survival in circulation, and colonization at distant sites, provides another tractable axis for therapeutic testing and biomarker development ref [38]. In parallel, macrophage-focused models have clarified how innate immune cells can be both therapeutic targets and delivery platforms, reinforcing the translational value of immune-competent CRC systems for evaluating combination strategies against metastatic disease ref [33].

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Experimental CRC models have become especially valuable for therapeutic development when they preserve the metastatic niche and stromal context, because these systems reveal liabilities that are not evident in tumor-cell monocultures. Metastasis models showed that colorectal cancer initiation in distant organs can depend on a TGF-β-driven program in stromal cells, supporting the rationale for therapies that target stromal signaling rather than only epithelial oncogenic drivers ref [12]. Likewise, single-cell dissection of CRC liver metastasis has mapped dynamic immune states across metastatic progression, providing a framework for testing immunomodulatory combinations and for stratifying patients according to metastatic immune ecosystems ref [27].

These platforms also clarify how stemness-associated subpopulations shape treatment response and relapse. Functional studies identified CD44v6-positive cells as metastasis-driving cancer stem cell states, while lineage-tracing approaches demonstrated a distinct contribution of Lgr5+ cells in primary versus metastatic colon cancer ref [23], ref [26]. Such findings support the use of organoids, xenografts, and metastatic transplantation models to evaluate therapies directed against stem-cell plasticity, metastatic seeding, and minimal residual disease. In parallel, noncoding regulators such as circCCDC66 have emerged from model-based studies as candidates for biomarker development and therapeutic intervention because they promote tumor growth and dissemination ref [36].

Another major application is the identification of microenvironment-mediated resistance mechanisms relevant to precision oncology. CRC models incorporating fibroblasts, macrophages, or extracellular vesicles showed that CAF-derived exosomes enhance stemness, epithelial-mesenchymal traits, metastasis, and chemotherapy resistance ref [28]. Similarly, co-culture and in vivo metastatic assays demonstrated that reciprocal signaling between tumor cells and tumor-associated macrophages is required for mesenchymal circulating tumor cell-mediated metastasis ref [25]. Together, these data argue that translational testing in multicellular CRC models can better predict response to combination regimens targeting tumor cells, stromal programs, and immune crosstalk simultaneously ref [12], ref [27], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Experimental models are particularly valuable for translational studies aimed at metastasis prevention and treatment stratification, because they permit functional interrogation of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), stemness, and phenotypic plasticity under controlled conditions. In colorectal cancer, these interconnected programs are increasingly viewed not only as drivers of dissemination but also as determinants of drug tolerance and relapse, making them attractive endpoints in organoid, xenograft, and co-culture platforms used for therapeutic testing ref [17], ref [22], ref [29].

Models enriched for cancer stem cell features have been used to evaluate agents that suppress tumor re-initiation, metastatic seeding, and post-therapy recurrence. This strategy is supported by the evolving concept that metastasis-competent cells represent dynamic stem-like states rather than a fixed population, implying that experimental systems must capture state transitions when assessing treatment response or resistance liabilities ref [22], ref [26]. Relatedly, EMT-focused CRC models help identify compounds that may reverse invasive phenotypes or sensitize cells to therapy, while also clarifying when partial EMT states contribute more to resistance than to overt metastatic efficiency ref [17], ref [29].

Precision oncology applications increasingly integrate these phenotypic assays with microenvironmental and systems-level analyses. Tumor–stromal interactions shape metastatic fitness and therapeutic vulnerability, so models incorporating fibroblasts, extracellular matrix cues, or niche signals are useful for prioritizing anti-metastatic combinations ref [36]. Single-cell profiling and systems biology further enhance these platforms by resolving intratumoral heterogeneity, lineage plasticity, and network-level resistance programs, thereby improving biomarker discovery and patient-specific prediction of metastatic behavior and treatment benefit ref [65], ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Experimental CRC models have also become important tools for evaluating microenvironment-directed and metastasis-preventive therapies, particularly in the context of liver dissemination. Comparative analyses of primary colorectal tumors and matched liver metastases reveal linked but dynamically remodeled immune phenotypes, indicating that translational models must capture both the primary lesion and the metastatic niche when testing immunomodulatory strategies ref [26]. In this setting, co-culture systems, orthotopic implantation, and metastasis models are especially valuable for identifying context-dependent therapeutic vulnerabilities that would be missed in tumor-cell-only assays.

A recurring theme across these models is the therapeutic relevance of stromal and myeloid reprogramming. Mesenchymal stem cells can enhance colon cancer growth and metastasis, supporting their use in experimental platforms designed to test stromal-targeting interventions ref [16]. Several studies further show that CRC progression is promoted by macrophage M2 polarization driven by distinct upstream signals, including gut microbiota-induced cathepsin K/TLR4 signaling, exosome-encapsulated miRNAs acting through the CXCL12/CXCR4 axis, and the lncRNA RPPH1-mediated exosomal communication network ref [17], ref [24], ref [28]. These findings provide a rationale for using complex CRC models to evaluate inhibitors of TLR4 signaling, macrophage polarization, chemokine axes, or extracellular vesicle trafficking as adjuncts to conventional therapy.

Metastasis-oriented models likewise help prioritize anti-adhesion and anti-colonization strategies. In human CRC cells, LPS-induced TLR4 signaling enhances beta1-integrin-mediated adhesion and promotes liver metastasis, illustrating how inflammatory cues can be converted into actionable therapeutic targets ref [38]. When integrated with immune-phenotype data from matched metastatic specimens ref [26], such models support precision-oncology workflows in which patients may be stratified not only by tumor genomics, but also by microenvironmental programs that predict response to immunotherapy, anti-inflammatory treatment, or combination regimens aimed at preventing metastatic outgrowth.

subsections.section_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology
subsections.subsection_title: Applications of Experimental Models in Therapeutic Development and Precision Oncology - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major translational use of colorectal cancer (CRC) experimental models is the functional dissection of metastatic liabilities that can be converted into therapeutic targets or response biomarkers. Metastasis-competent CRC models have shown that L1CAM is not only associated with dissemination but also marks regenerative, metastasis-initiating cell states, indicating that model systems can identify stem-like programs linked to relapse risk and potential targetability ref [26]. Earlier metastasis assays likewise demonstrated that coordinated expression of L1-CAM and ADAM10 enhances invasive and metastatic behavior, supporting their value as mechanistically grounded biomarkers for stratification and intervention ref [21].

These platforms are also useful for prioritizing pathway-directed therapies against specific prometastatic signaling circuits. In CRC models, tumor-derived CXCL5 drives metastasis through ERK/Elk-1/Snail and AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin signaling, illustrating how experimental systems can connect secreted factors to actionable downstream nodes and resistance-associated epithelial–mesenchymal plasticity ref [19]. Metabolic dependencies can be mapped in a similar way: hypoxia-induced glutaminase 1 is required for tumor growth, invasion, and metastatic colonization, suggesting that metabolic inhibition may be particularly relevant in aggressive, hypoxic disease states identified in preclinical testing ref [38].

Beyond cancer-cell intrinsic programs, experimental models increasingly support precision oncology by capturing stromal and intercellular determinants of therapeutic vulnerability. For example, cancer-derived exosomal HSPC111 promotes liver metastasis by reprogramming lipid metabolism in cancer-associated fibroblasts, highlighting exosome-mediated stromal education as both a biomarker source and a candidate intervention axis ref [23]. Collectively, these studies show that CRC models can nominate biomarkers of metastatic fitness, uncover resistance mechanisms rooted in plasticity, metabolism, and microenvironmental crosstalk, and thereby guide patient-tailored strategies that extend beyond conventional cytotoxic screening ref [19], ref [21], ref [23], ref [26], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A major limitation of current colorectal cancer (CRC) models is their incomplete representation of the tumor microenvironment, which is a dynamic regulator of invasion, metastatic competence, and therapeutic response rather than a passive backdrop. Conventional 2D cultures and even many organoid systems insufficiently capture stromal reciprocity, spatial gradients, and multicellular signaling, thereby reducing translational fidelity when modeling progression or drug sensitivity ref [49], ref [12].

This gap is especially evident for fibroblast, extracellular matrix, hypoxic, and immune components. Cancer-associated fibroblasts actively shape growth factor availability, matrix deposition, and paracrine resistance programs, yet their source, activation state, and co-culture ratios vary markedly across studies ref [9]. Likewise, extracellular matrix composition and remodeling are central determinants of migration, mechanotransduction, and colonization, but are often simplified to poorly defined basement-membrane extracts that obscure reproducibility ref [26]. Hypoxia further reprograms angiogenesis, metabolism, and therapy resistance, although oxygen tension is rarely standardized in vitro ref [29]. Immune representation is also limited: macrophage polarization states and T-cell memory compartments can critically influence CRC dissemination and outcome, but are seldom preserved in durable model systems ref [33], ref [19].

Future progress therefore depends on standardizing microenvironmental variables as explicit experimental parameters rather than background conditions. CRC platforms should incorporate defined stromal cell populations, tunable matrix properties, controlled oxygenation, and immune modules with documented cellular composition and functional readouts ref [49], ref [29], ref [33]. Mechanistically informed designs are particularly important for pathways such as TGFβ-mediated immune evasion, which illustrates how metastasis-relevant phenotypes emerge from tumor–stroma–immune crosstalk and can be missed in reductionist systems ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A major limitation of current colorectal cancer (CRC) models is their incomplete representation of metastatic niche complexity. Evidence from stromal-focused studies shows that metastasis initiation depends not only on intrinsic tumor programs but also on TGF-β-activated stromal states, macrophage–tumor crosstalk, and fibroblast-derived exosomal signaling that promotes stemness, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and drug resistance ref [12], ref [25], ref [28]. Models relying only on epithelial tumor cells therefore risk underestimating context-dependent vulnerabilities and overestimating treatment efficacy.

This problem is compounded by unresolved cellular heterogeneity. Metastatic competence in CRC is linked to dynamic stem-like populations marked by CD44v6 or Lgr5, yet these states are not static and may differ between primary tumors and metastatic lesions ref [23], ref [26]. Single-cell analysis of liver metastases further demonstrates marked spatiotemporal immune remodeling, underscoring that model systems lacking evolving immune architecture cannot faithfully capture progression or therapeutic response ref [27]. Standardization should thus extend beyond genetic background to include stromal composition, immune context, and metastatic site-specific readouts.

Future model development should integrate multicellular co-culture, organoid, and in vivo platforms with standardized single-cell and spatial profiling pipelines. Such frameworks would be better suited to track noncoding drivers, including circRNA-mediated programs such as CCDC66, alongside stemness and microenvironmental adaptation during metastatic evolution ref [36]. A key goal is to establish interoperable benchmark models that reproduce both tumor-intrinsic plasticity and host niche dependence, thereby improving translational validity for anti-metastatic and combination therapies ref [12], ref [27].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A major limitation of current colorectal cancer (CRC) models is their incomplete representation of the dynamic metastatic cascade, particularly the coupling among epithelial–mesenchymal plasticity, cell motility, and clonal diversification. Many reductionist systems capture proliferation or endpoint invasion, but fail to reproduce the transient and reversible cell-state transitions that govern dissemination and therapy adaptation in vivo. This is especially problematic because EMT in CRC is not a binary event, but a spectrum of regulatory states shaped by context, and because single-cell analyses have shown that metastatic competence emerges from highly heterogeneous tumor subpopulations rather than from a uniform invasive phenotype ref [17], ref [18].

Standardization is further complicated by the underappreciated influence of matrix architecture and stromal context. Extracellular matrix composition, stiffness, and remodeling are not passive background variables; they actively regulate adhesion, migration, invasion, and colonization, yet these parameters are inconsistently defined across organoid, spheroid, microfluidic, and xenograft platforms ref [14], ref [36]. Likewise, lessons from simple model organisms underscore that motility programs are governed by conserved cell-biophysical mechanisms that are often obscured in oversimplified CRC assays ref [25]. As a result, nominally similar models may generate divergent conclusions about invasion, metastatic potential, or drug response.

Future progress will require systems-level and multiscale experimental frameworks that integrate single-cell readouts, matrix-aware engineering, and computational modeling of metastasis as an evolving ecosystem ref [37], ref [18]. For CRC specifically, more predictive platforms should standardize ECM properties, quantify intermediate EMT states, and include stromal and biomechanical variables as reportable experimental metadata rather than optional add-ons ref [14], ref [17], ref [36]. Such approaches would improve cross-study reproducibility while better aligning experimental models with the biological complexity of metastatic CRC.

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A persistent limitation of colorectal cancer (CRC) models is their incomplete representation of metastatic niche education by immune, stromal, microbial, and vesicle-mediated signals. Available studies show that macrophage polarization is strongly shaped by tumor-derived exosomes and noncoding RNAs, with exosome-encapsulated miRNAs and lncRNA RPPH1 both promoting M2-like states linked to CRC dissemination and liver colonization, yet these interactions are often absent from standard monoculture or even many organoid systems [24, 28]. Likewise, mesenchymal stem cells can enhance colon cancer growth and metastasis, underscoring how stromal cell composition can substantially alter experimental phenotypes [16].

Modeling the gut-liver axis remains especially challenging. Microbiota-driven inflammatory signaling has been implicated in metastatic progression, including gut microbiota-stimulated cathepsin K secretion that promotes TLR4-dependent M2 macrophage polarization, and LPS-TLR4 signaling in CRC cells that increases beta1 integrin-mediated adhesion and liver metastasis [17, 38]. These findings indicate that metastatic behavior depends not only on tumor-intrinsic genetics but also on microbial products and host innate immune circuitry, variables that are rarely standardized across animal facilities, donor-derived platforms, or co-culture protocols.

Future CRC modeling should therefore move toward modular but standardized multi-compartment systems integrating tumor cells, stromal populations, myeloid subsets, extracellular vesicles, and microbiota-derived cues. Comparative benchmarking against clinical immune states is also needed, because immune phenotypic linkage analyses suggest that primary CRC and matched liver metastases share but also remodel immune programs during progression [4]. Incorporating such matched primary-metastatic immune readouts into model validation would improve translational relevance and help define which platforms truly capture metastatic ecosystem dynamics rather than only tumor cell proliferation [4, 16, 17, 24, 28, 38].

subsections.section_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Current Limitations, Standardization Challenges, and Future Directions in CRC Experimental Modeling - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A persistent limitation of current colorectal cancer (CRC) models is their weak representation of metastatic initiation and colonization as ecosystem-level processes rather than purely tumor cell-intrinsic events. Work on metastasis-initiating cells emphasizes that dissemination depends on rare, plastic cell states embedded within supportive niches, while CRC-specific studies identify regenerative L1CAM-positive populations as key drivers of metastatic outgrowth [ref 4, ref 26, ref 39]. These observations expose a translational gap in conventional 2D cultures, many organoid systems, and short-term xenografts, which often preserve proliferative capacity but incompletely capture stemness plasticity, dormancy-to-reactivation transitions, and the selective pressures that shape metastatic competence.

Standardization is further challenged by the inadequate modeling of stromal, biophysical, and metabolic determinants of CRC progression. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) actively regulate invasion and metastatic seeding, and CRC-derived exosomal signals can reprogram CAF lipid metabolism to facilitate liver metastasis, indicating that stromal state must be treated as an experimental variable rather than background noise [ref 23, ref 35]. Likewise, matrix mechanics, interstitial forces, and other biophysical properties strongly influence metastatic behavior, yet are rarely harmonized across platforms [ref 16]. Hypoxia-driven metabolic rewiring, including glutaminase 1 induction, and prometastatic cytokine signaling such as CXCL5-mediated activation of ERK/Elk-1/Snail and AKT/GSK3β/β-catenin pathways further underscore that microenvironmental context is inseparable from invasive phenotype [ref 19, ref 38].

Future CRC modeling should therefore move toward standardized multi-compartment systems that integrate metastasis-initiating cell states, stromal co-cultures, tunable mechanics, and organotropic metastatic niches. Priority directions include benchmarked co-culture protocols with defined CAF phenotypes, reporting standards for oxygen tension and extracellular matrix mechanics, and longitudinal readouts of metastatic regeneration rather than primary tumor growth alone [ref 16, ref 23, ref 35]. Such frameworks would better align experimental models with the ecosystem view of metastasis and improve prediction of clinically relevant metastatic liabilities in CRC [ref 4, ref 39].
